result: The rnts>eiger genetic system induces temporally-controlled tissue ablation in the wing pouch, which typically regenerates to produce viable adults with normal wings. However, in some genetic backgrounds, ectopic wings and ectopic pouches are observed following ablation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 describe the experimental system and its typical outcomes, supported by both text descriptions and visual evidence in Figure 1. The system is well-established (C1), normal regeneration is documented (C2-C3), and ectopic wing formation in certain backgrounds is clearly shown (C4-C5).

result: A systematic screen of 226 deletions covering ~90% of chromosome 3 identified multiple deletions that enhance ectopic wing formation, with varying penetrance from low (<10%) to high (>25%).
evaluation: Claims C6-C9 describe the screening approach and results, with explicit quantification of the number of deletions tested (C7), genomic coverage (C8), and distribution of phenotypic classes (C9). The data are presented in Figure 1H-K with clear numerical support.

result: CtBP was identified as the gene responsible for enhancing ectopic wing formation. Multiple CtBP alleles (deletion, hypomorphic, and loss-of-function) caused ectopic wings at frequencies ranging from 22-47%, while mock ablation controls showed no ectopic wings.
evaluation: Claims C10-C14 establish CtBP as the causal gene through testing of multiple alleles with consistent phenotypes (C11-C13) and appropriate negative controls (C14). The data in Figure 2A provide quantitative support with sample sizes indicated.

result: The highest frequency of ectopic wings in CtBP mutants occurred when damage was initiated on day 7 AEL, while wild type showed no ectopic wings at any developmental stage tested.
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 describe the developmental timing dependence of the phenotype, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The comparison between mutant and wild type across multiple time points provides clear evidence for the developmental specificity.

result: CtBP is a transcriptional co-repressor that does not bind DNA directly but associates with DNA-binding proteins via PxDLS motifs. Drosophila has a single CtBP gene with multiple isoforms grouped as short or long forms.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 provide background knowledge about CtBP, supported by multiple citations to established literature. The description of isoforms (C23) is supported by Figure 2C showing the protein structure.

result: CRISPR/Cas9-generated CtBP alleles on an isogenic background confirmed that CtBP disruption causes ectopic wings. A hypomorphic allele (CtBPN148PY) induced EWs in ~11% of adults, while a suspected null (CtBP148Δ2) induced EWs in ~20% of adults.
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 describe the CRISPR validation experiments with appropriate controls (C25) and multiple alleles showing dose-dependent effects (C27-C28). Figure 2D provides quantitative data supporting the phenotypic frequencies. The use of an isogenic background strengthens the conclusion that CtBP is responsible.

result: Following damage, both wild type and CtBP mutant discs show apoptosis and high Wg expression around the damaged pouch. However, ~45% of CtBP mutant discs show ectopic Wg expression in the notum at 0 hr recovery, which develops into an ectopic pouch over 24-48 hr.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe early molecular events in ectopic pouch formation, supported by Figure 3A-F showing Wg and apoptosis patterns at multiple time points. The quantification of frequency (~45%) and temporal progression are clearly documented.

result: The damage-dependent wg enhancer (BRV-B-GFP) is JNK-dependent and drives reporter expression at the site of ectopic pouch formation in CtBP mutants but not wild type. Removal of one copy of this enhancer reduces ectopic wing frequency.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 establish the role of the damage-dependent wg enhancer, supported by Figure 3G-I showing reporter expression patterns and genetic manipulation results. The consistency with prior work (C41) strengthens the interpretation.

result: Wg expression during second instar can trigger ectopic wings, but expression during third instar cannot. Overexpression of Wg alone or with egr does not enhance ectopic wing frequency, suggesting other pathways are required.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 demonstrate developmental stage-specific requirements for Wg-induced fate changes, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3J. The negative results with Wg overexpression (C45) are important for ruling out simple Wg sufficiency.

result: JNK pathway indicators (AP-1-RFP and MMP1) are expressed at the site of ectopic pouch formation in CtBP mutants at 0 hr and 48 hr recovery, suggesting JNK activity is important for triggering ectopic wing pouch formation.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 establish JNK pathway activation at the ectopic site, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The temporal and spatial correlation between JNK markers and ectopic pouch formation supports the inference (C50).

result: dilp8 is upregulated during transdetermination and regeneration. Following damage, dilp8-GFP is expressed around the regenerating pouch and, in CtBP mutants, at a second spot in the notum that overlaps with increased Wg expression and persists through ectopic pouch formation.
evaluation: Claims C51-C59 establish dilp8 as an early marker of ectopic pouch formation, supported by Figure 3K-N showing expression patterns at multiple time points. The spatial overlap with Wg (C58) and temporal persistence (C59) are clearly documented.

result: dilp8-GFP expression in the notum overlaps with MMP1 expression, consistent with JNK contributing to dilp8 expression. dilp8-GFP is expressed in cells still expressing notum markers before pouch markers appear, suggesting it is an early marker of fate change.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 establish the relationship between JNK activity and dilp8 expression and its role as an early fate change marker. Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and 3 provide supporting evidence for the spatial overlap and marker expression patterns.

result: The frequency of secondary dilp8-GFP spots in discs (~40% in CtBP mutants, 0% in wild type) matches the frequency of ectopic wings per heminotum in adults, indicating dilp8-GFP is a predictive early marker.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 establish the quantitative correlation between early dilp8-GFP expression and adult ectopic wing phenotype, supported by Figure 3O. The consistency across time points and match with adult frequencies strongly support the predictive value.

result: Bilateral ectopic wings occur slightly more frequently than expected for independent events, possibly due to identical disc timing or circulating factors.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 describe the bilateral frequency and speculate on mechanisms. Figure 3—figure supplement 4 provides the quantitative comparison. However, C68 is speculative and no direct evidence for the proposed mechanisms is provided.

result: dilp8 loss-of-function mutants lack ectopic wings, while UAS-dilp8 overexpression enhances ectopic wing frequency without triggering them alone, suggesting developmental delay mediated by Dilp8 is important for ectopic wing formation.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 establish the requirement for dilp8 function, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 5. The genetic manipulation results (loss and gain of function) provide strong evidence for the role of developmental delay (C71).

result: Marked clones in the ectopic pouch are arranged radially but occupy only ~10% of the pouch, suggesting the ectopic pouch arises from multiple cells changing fate simultaneously or by progressive recruitment.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 describe clonal analysis results supported by Figure 4A. The observation that clones are small relative to the ectopic pouch size supports the inference of multi-cell origin, though the exact mechanism (simultaneous vs. progressive) cannot be distinguished.

result: Lineage tracing with R76B02-lexA and other notum-specific lexA lines shows that cells in the ectopic pouch once expressed notum markers, indicating they underwent a notum-to-pouch fate change.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76 establish the notum origin of ectopic pouch cells through lineage tracing, supported by Figure 4B-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The use of multiple independent lexA lines (C76) strengthens the conclusion.

result: The ectopic Wg expression occurs within the mirr-lacZ domain (notum), and removing one copy of mirr increases ectopic wing frequency in both wild type and CtBP mutants, suggesting reduced notum-specifying factors increase susceptibility to fate change.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 establish the role of notum identity factors in resisting fate change, supported by Figure 4D-G. The genetic interaction between mirr and CtBP (C81) and the inference about notum-specifying factors (C82) are well-supported.

result: The ectopic pouch is composed of both anterior and posterior cells, with initial events occurring in the posterior compartment. dilp8-GFP expression begins posteriorly and spreads to anterior cells. Clones do not cross the compartment boundary, indicating the ectopic pouch arises from both A and P precursors that preserve compartmental identity.
evaluation: Claims C83-C92 establish the compartmental composition and origin of the ectopic pouch through multiple lines of evidence: dilp8-GFP expression patterns (C85-C87), quantification of compartmental location (C86), and clonal analysis (C88). Figure 4H-K provides strong supporting data.

result: JNK signaling is increased in the notum during early ectopic pouch development. The system uses Egr (Drosophila TNF-α) to activate JNK-dependent apoptosis, and JNK may function in multiple ways to promote fate change.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 summarize the role of JNK signaling, supported by earlier data on AP-1-RFP and MMP1 expression. The citation for Egr function (C94) and the inference about multiple JNK functions (C95) are reasonable given the data.

result: Reducing JNK signaling (by removing one copy of hep or expressing dominant negative JNK or Fos) reduces or eliminates ectopic wing formation, indicating JNK/AP-1 signaling is required for ectopic wing generation.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 establish the requirement for JNK/AP-1 signaling through genetic manipulation, supported by Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The complete suppression with dominant negatives (C97) provides strong evidence for necessity.

result: Ablation alone (via rpr) or constitutive JNK activation (via hepCA) is insufficient to produce ectopic wings. Shortening the ablation period reduces ectopic wing frequency for egr but not for rpr or hepCA.
evaluation: Claims C100-C104 demonstrate that specific aspects of Egr signaling beyond simple apoptosis or JNK activation are required, supported by Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The comparison across different damage methods is well-controlled.

result: Egr signals through Grindelwald to activate JNK, but overexpression of the Grind intracellular domain does not produce ectopic wings. A secreted form of Egr is more effective than membrane-tethered Egr, suggesting local spread of Egr is necessary.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 dissect the Egr signaling requirements, supported by Figure 5B. The comparison between different forms of Egr and Grind activation provides evidence that additional aspects of Egr signaling beyond Grind are required.

result: rn-GAL4 is expressed in the wing pouch, myoblasts, and scattered notum cells. Egr expression in the pouch is critical for ectopic wing formation, while expression in notum or myoblasts alone is insufficient.
evaluation: Claims C109-C111 define the spatial requirements for Egr expression, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3. The use of different GAL4 drivers to test sufficiency in different domains provides clear evidence for the pouch requirement.

result: Reducing apoptosis (by removing pro-apoptotic genes or expressing caspase inhibitors) does not affect ectopic wing frequency, while increasing apoptosis suppresses ectopic wings. This suggests a population of cells with high JNK but delayed death is needed, possibly as a source of diffusible factors.
evaluation: Claims C112-C117 dissect the relationship between apoptosis and JNK signaling, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and 5. The bidirectional manipulation of apoptosis and the observation of surviving Egr-expressing cells (C117) support the inference about diffusible factors (C116).

result: CtBP expression is uniform in wing discs. Rescue occurs with ubiquitous but not pouch-specific CtBP expression, and CtBP knockdown in the pouch does not cause ectopic wings, suggesting CtBP functions outside the pouch, possibly in the notum.
evaluation: Claims C118-C121 establish the spatial requirement for CtBP function through expression analysis and rescue experiments, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 6. The combination of rescue and knockdown experiments provides strong evidence for the notum requirement.

result: CtBP mutant clones autonomously upregulate AP-1 targets (AP-1-GFP, dilp8-GFP, MMP1-lacZ) without causing apoptosis or elevated MMP1 protein. Activation is non-uniform and higher in the hinge, suggesting CtBP reduction enhances JNK signaling in specific regions.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 establish the cell-autonomous effect of CtBP loss on AP-1 targets, supported by Figure 5G-I and Figure 5—figure supplement 7. The regional variation in activation (C123) is an important observation for understanding the spatial specificity of the phenotype.

result: Upd family ligands are promoted by JNK signaling. Co-expression of UAS-upd1 with rnts>egr dramatically increases ectopic wing frequency to ~17% in wild type and ~90% in CtBP mutants, with 85% of discs showing large ectopic pouches.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 establish the synergistic effect of Upd1 and Egr, supported by Figure 6A-B. The dramatic increase in frequency and the high penetrance of ectopic pouches in discs provide strong evidence for the importance of JAK/STAT signaling.

result: JAK/STAT signaling (measured by STAT-DGFP) is higher in early L3 than late L3 discs. After damage, STAT-DGFP is expressed around the ablated pouch in wild type, but in CtBP mutants, a patch of STAT-DGFP is also detected in the notum, suggesting JAK/STAT may induce fate change.
evaluation: Claims C128-C131 establish the spatial and temporal patterns of JAK/STAT activity, supported by Figure 6C-F. The ectopic STAT activity in the notum of CtBP mutants (C130) is a key observation linking JAK/STAT to fate change.

result: STAT-DGFP expression often overlaps with MMP1 expression, but in some CtBP mutant discs, STAT-DGFP is detected without MMP1, suggesting JAK/STAT activity can occur independently of ectopic JNK activation.
evaluation: Claims C132-C133 establish the relationship between JAK/STAT and JNK activities, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The observation of STAT activity without MMP1 (C133) is important for understanding the independence of these pathways.

result: Upd ligands are upregulated following damage. upd3-lacZ is expressed in the ablated pouch region but not in the notum where STAT-DGFP is detected, suggesting Upd ligands produced in the pouch diffuse to activate JAK/STAT in the notum.
evaluation: Claims C134-C136 establish the source of Upd ligands through reporter analysis, supported by Figure 6G-I. The speculation about diffusion (C137) is reasonable given the known properties of Upd ligands and the spatial separation of ligand production and STAT activity.

result: UAS-upd1 expression in myoblasts activates JAK/STAT in the notum and disrupts the notum Wg stripe but does not form an ectopic pouch. Similar Wg stripe disruption occurs after rnts>egr damage, suggesting Wg stripe disruption alone is insufficient for ectopic pouch formation.
evaluation: Claims C138-C140 demonstrate that JAK/STAT activation alone is insufficient for fate change, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3D. This is an important negative result establishing the requirement for multiple pathways.

result: Removing one copy of Stat92E or Upd ligands (upd2, upd3) significantly reduces ectopic wing frequency. Rescue by UAS-upd1 indicates Upd family ligands act similarly. Together, this shows JAK/STAT signaling levels modulate notum-to-pouch fate change frequency.
evaluation: Claims C141-C144 establish the requirement for JAK/STAT signaling through genetic manipulation, supported by Figure 6J-K. The dose-dependent effects and rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the modulatory role of JAK/STAT.

result: upd3 expression is not altered in CtBP mutant clones, but STAT-DGFP shows a slight increase in young discs in regions where the pathway is normally active, suggesting CtBP reduction makes tissues more responsive to JAK/STAT.
evaluation: Claims C145-C147 establish that CtBP affects JAK/STAT responsiveness rather than ligand production, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and 4. The regional and temporal specificity of the effect (C146) is consistent with the overall model.

result: UAS-upd1 expression along the A-P boundary or in random clones specifically activates dilp8-GFP in a region of the notum similar to where ectopic pouches form. dpp>upd1 activates STAT-DGFP only in specific notum and pouch regions, indicating a notum region specifically responsive to Upd ligands. However, Upd1 alone without JNK activation is insufficient for fate change.
evaluation: Claims C148-C152 identify a 'weak point' in the notum that is specifically responsive to Upd ligands, supported by Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The negative result with Upd1 alone (C152) reinforces the requirement for both JNK and JAK/STAT pathways.

result: Regeneration requires cells to change fates to replace damaged tissue. The limited plasticity necessary for regeneration results from an interplay between pathways promoting plasticity (JNK/AP-1, JAK/STAT) and regulators limiting their activity (CtBP). Both JNK/AP-1 and JAK/STAT activation appear necessary for notum-to-pouch fate change.
evaluation: Claims C153-C156 present the main conceptual framework and conclusions of the study, synthesizing the experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the extensive genetic and molecular data showing requirements for both pathways and the role of CtBP in limiting plasticity.

result: Neither rpr-mediated ablation nor Grind activation suffices for ectopic wings, indicating Egr activates additional pathways or acts outside the rn-GAL4 domain. Secreted Egr is more effective than membrane-tethered form. CtBP reduction likely makes the notum more responsive to Egr signaling, and increased JNK in dying pouch cells would generate Upd ligands.
evaluation: Claims C157-C164 synthesize the mechanistic understanding of how damage signals from the pouch to the notum. The inferences are well-supported by the experimental data, though some aspects (C159-C160) remain speculative. The model is internally consistent and explains the observed phenomena.

result: Increased STAT activity reduces notum-specific gene expression. Reducing mirr dosage increases ectopic wing frequency. A recent study reported ectopic wings from UAS-upd1 expression in the notum during second instar, which may also involve combined JAK/STAT and AP-1 activation due to apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C165-C170 integrate the current findings with prior work and discuss alternative interpretations. The citation of supporting literature (C165, C167) and the observation of apoptosis with Upd1 overexpression (C169) support the speculation about the mechanism in the other study (C170).

result: Imaginal discs have 'weak points' where fate changes occur preferentially. In the leg disc, the weak point is where Wg and Dpp are co-expressed. In the wing disc, the AP and DV boundaries likely intersect in the notum near where ectopic pouches form. This region may be predisposed to STAT activity and is specifically responsive to Upd ligands.
evaluation: Claims C171-C181 develop the 'weak point' hypothesis by analogy to prior work and integration with the current findings. The spatial analysis of morphogen expression (C174-C175) and the demonstration of specific Upd responsiveness (C179-C181) support the model, though some aspects remain speculative (C177-C178).

result: Recent studies identified tumor hot-spots and apoptosis-resistant regions in wing discs with elevated JAK/STAT activity, suggesting regions with elevated STAT may be more capable of surviving damage and re-specifying fates.
evaluation: Claims C182-C183 integrate recent literature with the current findings to support the model. The citations provide independent support for the role of JAK/STAT in cell survival and fate plasticity.

result: During normal development, wing pouch specification occurs in first instar when STAT is active throughout the disc and wg is expressed in a patch. Wg expression expands through feed-forward recruitment. In the regeneration system, wg expression from the damage-responsive enhancer is important, but Wg alone is insufficient. JAK/STAT and AP-1 activity reduce notum-specific genes, creating conditions similar to early pouch specification.
evaluation: Claims C184-C193 draw parallels between normal development and damage-induced fate change, supported by citations to developmental literature and the experimental findings. The model that JAK/STAT and AP-1 create a permissive state for Wg-mediated fate change (C193) integrates the findings into a coherent developmental framework.

result: Once the ectopic pouch is specified, it may activate rn-GAL4, leading to egr expression, localized apoptosis and JNK activation. Surrounding cells would activate AP-1 and STAT and express wg, reinforcing conditions for fate change. A recent paper supports damage-induced fate changes relying on JAK/STAT and Wg signaling.
evaluation: Claims C194-C197 present a speculative model for how the ectopic pouch is reinforced, marked as speculation in the evidence. While the model is plausible and consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental support. The citation of supporting work (C198) adds some credibility but does not validate the specific mechanism proposed.

result: CtBP mutant clones have elevated AP-1 activity and, in some regions, increased STAT activity. CtBP interacts with multiple transcriptional repressors via PxDLS motifs. Some Kayak (Fos) isoforms have PxDLS motifs, suggesting AP-1 may repress target genes via CtBP in the absence of activating signals, buffering fates from JNK fluctuations.
evaluation: Claims C199-C200 summarize the CtBP findings, well-supported by the data. Claims C201-C203 present a speculative molecular mechanism for how CtBP might regulate AP-1 activity. While the presence of PxDLS motifs in Kayak (C201) is factual, the proposed mechanism (C202-C203) is speculative and lacks direct experimental support.
